title: Common Prompting Mistakes
hook: Most 'AI is useless' moments trace back to a handful of fixable habits: asking too vaguely, dumping everything at once, and accepting the first draft as final.
key_points: Too vague: 'write something about X' gives generic mush — add audience, goal, length.
All at once: cramming ten requirements into one prompt; break it into steps.
No example: not showing what 'good' looks like when you easily could.
One-and-done: taking the first answer instead of asking for a revision.
content_html: When people bounce off AI, the culprit is usually the prompt, not the tool — and the mistakes are predictable. The biggest is being too vague: "write something about productivity" gives the model nothing to aim at, so it returns bland, forgettable filler. The fix is context — who it's for, what it's meant to do, how long, what angle. A second common trap is dumping everything at once: ten requirements crammed into one paragraph, where the model quietly drops half of them. Breaking a big ask into steps ("first outline it, then we'll draft section by section") works far better.
extra_html: Two more habits quietly cost people the best results. Not showing an example — if you have a sample email, a style you like, or a format you want, paste it; models are superb at matching a pattern and weak at guessing one. And treating the first answer as final — the first draft is a starting point, not a verdict. Saying "too formal, loosen it up" or "cut this in half and lead with the conclusion" steers it in seconds. None of this is special "prompt engineering"; it's the same clarity you'd use briefing a capable assistant who can't read your mind. Fix these four and the same tool that felt useless starts feeling indispensable.

related.title: Talking to AI
related.hook: The difference between a useless answer and a great one is usually the question. Give the AI context, an example, and a clear job — and treat it as a conversation, not a vending machine.

related.title: Chatbots & Assistants
related.hook: ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini feel like talking to a person, but they're generative AI with a chat wrapper — brilliant writing partners, unreliable encyclopedias.

related.title: When AI Makes Things Up
related.hook: AI 'hallucinations' aren't glitches — they're the technology working as designed. A model that always predicts a plausible next word will sometimes produce a plausible falsehood.

flashcards.prompt: Why does 'write something about climate change' usually disappoint?

choices.text: It's too vague — no audience, goal, length, or angle to work from
The topic is too hard for AI

flashcards.explanation_html: With nothing to aim at, the model defaults to generic filler. Naming the reader, purpose, length, and angle is what makes the output useful.

flashcards.prompt: What should you do instead of accepting a mediocre first answer?
flashcards.back_html: Ask for a revision — "shorter," "more concrete," "in a warmer tone," "add an example." Iterating is part of using AI well, not a failure.
